# The name Haoma and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Haoma** opens onto ​the domain of sacred plant, immortality, the Zoroastrian tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post moves through that world room by room — the name and its roots, the ‌original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, and its afterlife — before arriving at the digital temple that makes the record addressable. The letters are plain; the ‌evidence is not.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Haoma
- **ASCII form:** haoma
- **Meaning:** "The pressed one"
- **Domain of influence:** Sacred Plant, Immortality
- **Pantheon:** Zoroastrian

- **Original script:** 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀 (Avestan)

## Overview

​**Haoma** (*haoma*) — Sacred Plant, Immortality · The pressed one — belongs to the Zoroastrian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sacred Plant, Immortality". The name means "The pressed one".

​**Haoma** is the deified sacred plant of Zoroastrianism, pressed at the dawn liturgy into the draught that grants vigor, wisdom, and a share in immortality. Green and golden-eyed, hymned as a yazata ​in his own right, he is the tradition's living sacrament — god, offering, and medicine crushed in a single mortar — and the Iranian double of the Vedic soma.

PuniCodex records the ​canonical scholarly spelling **Haoma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/haoma/). ## Mythology

The stories of Haoma place sacred plant, immortality at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Haoma appears in zoroastrian tradition ​as sacred plant, immortality. The name's meaning, "The pressed one", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Haoma in ritual, text, and iconography, ​ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Haoma survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, ​and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Haoma gives the figure a stable name around which ​these variants orbit.

### Haoma Who Was First Pressed (Yašt 9)

The ninth Yašt is the hymn of the plant made god: Haoma, green and with golden eyes, who was first pressed on ‌the heights of Hara (Yašt 9.16, 19). The Avesta remembers him as both herb and yazata — the only deity of the Iranian pantheon who is simultaneously the offering itself, pounded fresh ​on the pestle each night in the Yasna. His first-pressing on Hara Berezaiti, the Alborz, the axis of the world, is the same mountain where Mithra keeps his thousand-eared, thousand-eyed watch (Yašt ‌10.13) — sacrament and covenant share one summit. His color and eyes passed into iconography: the golden-green plant appears on Sasanian silver among the emblems of the consecrated banquet. **Haoma collapses the ​distance between altar and deity: the offering does not merely represent the god — it is the god, crushed to give life**.

### Zarathustra's Reproach and the Roll of the Righteous (Yasna 9)

The ‌most human scene in the Avesta opens the ninth chapter of the Yasna. Zarathuštra reproaches the plant: the karpans and the kavis — the sacrificial guilds he condemns — pressed you, Haoma, ​for the stupefying draught, and the plant stands accused by its own prophet (Yasna 9.1–3). Haoma answers with a catalogue of the righteous who pressed him rightly: Yima, who won the sun; ‌Thraētaona, who struck down the three-mouthed Aži Dahāka; Kərəsāspa, who slew the horned dragon Gandarəβa; and Vīštāspa, who first confessed the good religion (Yasna 9.3–8). The exchange is unique — a prophet ​interrogating his own sacrament — and its verdict is exact: The scene gives the tradition its own charter myth of ritual reform, rare in the ancient world. **the plant is holy; the ‌abuse is in the pressing. Ritual ethics, not chemistry, decides what a sacrament does to the soul**.

### The Draught of Vīštāspa (Yašt 9)

For King Vīštāspa, Haoma was oracles and victory. In ​Yašt 9 the king offers the plant the sacrifice of a hundred stallions, a hundred oxen, a hundred rams, and a hundred loads of grain — and the hymn says Haoma grants ​him what armies could not buy: the most fortunate of thoughts and the most victorious of weapons, with foreknowledge of the coming war against the Turanians and their daeva-worshipping king Arjāsp (Yašt ‌9.26–30). When Vīštāspa drank the pressed haoma, his spirit was illumined and his enemies' devices laid bare; the same hymn remembers the plant's gifts of swift horses and vanquishing glory. The myth ‌dignifies strategy as piety: **the visionary draught makes foresight itself a weapon, and the patron king who drinks it fights with wisdom before he fights with armies**.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography ‌associated with Haoma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Haoma, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Sacred ​Plant, Immortality

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Haoma across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim ​about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Haoma carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The green stalk with golden eyes** — His Avestan self-description — the mountain herb that is ‌simultaneously a god (Yašt 9.19)
- **The mortar and pestle** — The pounding-stone of the Yasna, where god, offering, and congregation meet nightly (Yasna 9–11)
- **The white haoma (parahōm)** — The paradisal plant of ​the renovation, drunk by the resurrected that they shall not die again (Bundahišn 30)
- **Spring water and milk** — The two companions of the pressing — purity and nourishment joined in the ​consecrated draught
- **Mount Hara (Alborz)** — The cosmic axis where the first pressing happened and Mithra keeps his watch — the sacrament's original altar (Yašt 9.16; 10.13)

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, ‌inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Haoma with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Zoroastrian name of this type the material record is ​expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions ​naming 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀, sanctuary or cult remains tied to sacred plant and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before ‌entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Haoma** is sacred plant, immortality. The name means "The pressed one" and belongs to the zoroastrian tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Haoma returns the figure ​to scholarly recognition.

### Sacred Plant

Central domain: sacred plant, immortality.

### Living Tradition

Honored in zoroastrian myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Canonical Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple with its canonical scholarly spelling ‌and supporting evidence.

### The First Pressing

On the heights of Hara the green, golden-eyed plant was first pressed — the primordial sacrament of the Avesta (Yašt 9.16).

### Right Pressing, Wrong Pressing

Zarathuštra ​reproaches Haoma for the draught of the false priests; the plant answers with a roll of righteous pressers (Yasna 9.3–8).

### The Visionary Draught

For King Vīštāspa's hundredfold sacrifice, Haoma grants foreknowledge of ​the war and 'the most victorious of weapons' (Yašt 9.26).

### The Living Yasna

The nightly pounding of twigs with water and milk — performed for millennia, and still performed today (Yasna 9–11).

## ​A Meditation

Haoma asks what a sacrament is. Not a symbol, exactly — the plant is eaten; not a drug alone — the ethics police it; not a metaphor — the god ​answers back. The rite's deepest claim is that matter can be holy without ceasing to be matter: water, twigs, milk, prayer, a mortar, a morning. In an age that splits body and ‌meaning into separate compartments, Haoma's nightly chemistry lesson endures: what you take in shapes what you are, and a tradition that has blessed its breakfast for four thousand years knows something about ‌slow transformation.
